subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Meeting with the Frog's Voice

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the poem by asking students what they know about frogs — where they live, what sounds they make. Students share freely in one or two words each.
Textbook pp.55–56: The teacher reads the entire poem aloud with clear expression, pausing at each stanza. Students follow in their books and listen for the frog's feelings and actions.
The teacher re-reads stanza by stanza. After each stanza, students are invited to name one thing the frog does or feels, building a shared picture of the poem's world.
Students read the poem aloud together as a class in a whole-group choral read. The teacher coaches for rhythm, noting how the rhyming couplets give the poem a bouncy, hopping feel.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the students' first full encounter with the poem, so lingering on expression and rhythm matters more than comprehension detail at this stage. The poem's bouncy rhyming couplets naturally invite a physical sense of hopping — let students sway or tap lightly as they read chorally. The textbook page spread (pp.55–56) should remain open throughout.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Frog's Life: Comprehension Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.56): answer questions on the frog's habitat, tongue, movement, and camouflage.

time_bands.activity: Students do a quick paired chant of the poem from memory — one partner reads odd stanzas, the other reads even stanzas. This refreshes the text before discussion.
Let us Think — A. (p.56): the teacher asks where the frog likes to sit or spend time. Pairs discuss; the class shares answers; the teacher draws out evidence from specific stanzas.

Let us Think — A. (p.56): the teacher asks how the frog catches its food and how it moves in water and on land. Students locate the relevant lines in the poem, discuss with a partner, and share whole-class.

Let us Think — A. (p.56): the teacher asks what helps the frog hide. Students identify the camouflage image (colours matching plants and leaves) and explain in their own words. The teacher summarises key observations on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate the frog's camouflage colours with its actual colour — the poem says colours match the surroundings, not that the frog is green. Prompt students to read the exact lines rather than recall from general knowledge. All four questions in Let us Think — A. are anchored here; the textbook page should be open throughout.

periods.activity_title: Thinking and Talking: The Frog's World and Ours

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.56): discuss frog-life feelings, hopping fun, frog-vs-fish, and webbed-feet comparison.

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the first prompt from p.56: what would it feel like to live both in water and on land? Students think silently for a moment, then share with a partner.
Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.56): pairs discuss the hopping prompt — if you could hop as high as a frog, what fun things would you do? Two or three students share with the class.

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.56): the teacher guides a whole-class discussion comparing a frog's life with a fish's life, drawing on the poem's images of land, water, dew, and ponds to anchor the comparison.

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.56): the teacher introduces the webbed-feet/flipper comparison prompt. Students discuss in pairs and then share; the teacher helps connect the frog's anatomy from the poem to a real-world parallel.

periods.teacher_notes: The frog-versus-fish comparison (prompt 3) often yields very brief answers — guide students to use the poem's specific details (webbed feet, croaking, living on land) to build richer contrasts. The flipper comparison (prompt 4) is a connecting prompt; accept reasonable real-world links and probe for the underlying idea of water-propulsion. Unanchored oracy tasks from this cell (tongue-twister drill and listen-and-repeat) will be covered in the next oracy unit.

periods.activity_title: Tongue Twisters and Sound Pairs: Frog-Themed Oracy Drill

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak — A. (p.58): tongue-twister drill — say each twister slowly, then faster.
Let us Listen — B. (p.58): teacher reads vowel-contrast word pairs; students listen and repeat.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the three tongue twisters on p.58 by reading each one once at a clear, slow pace. Students listen and follow in their books.

Let us Speak — A. (p.58): the class practises each tongue twister together — slow, then medium, then fast. Students count how many times they say it correctly; a few volunteers demonstrate their best run.

Let us Listen — B. (p.58): the teacher reads each vowel-contrast word pair aloud (bet–bat, set–sat, men–man, leg–lag, met–mat) two to three times. Students listen carefully and repeat each pair together, attending to the short vowel shift.

Students pair up. One partner says a word from a pair (e.g. 'bet') and the other points to or says its contrast partner ('bat'). They swap roles and repeat. The teacher circulates and corrects gently.

periods.teacher_notes: The tongue twisters all use 'fr' and 'fl' initial clusters — connect this to the frog poem's own language if students notice the pattern. For the vowel-pair discrimination, the e/a contrast (bet/bat, set/sat) is the most common source of confusion at this stage; give extra repetitions to those pairs. Both tasks are oral and require no written output.

periods.activity_title: My Frog's World: Listening, Drawing, and Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen — My Frog's World (p.60): follow teacher's instructions to draw a frog's world, label with poem words, and colour.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the full set of My Frog's World instructions aloud from p.60, once slowly. Students listen without drawing yet, building a mental picture of what they will create.
The teacher re-reads instruction 1 (draw the place) and instruction 2 (draw the frog in the setting) one at a time, pausing after each. Students begin their drawing in the space on p.60.

The teacher reads instruction 3 (decorate with words from the poem) aloud again. Students browse the poem on pp.55–56 for words that describe the frog's life and write selected words around their drawing.

Students colour their drawings following instruction 4. Two or three volunteers share their Frog's World with the class, reading out the words they chose. The teacher invites brief comments from the audience.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening strand here is instruction-following: students hear the teacher read the task steps and act on each one sequentially. Encourage students to choose words directly from the poem text (pp.55–56) rather than from memory alone, so the activity doubles as unhurried re-reading. Sharing at the end is brief — one or two sentences per student is sufficient.

periods.activity_title: Conjunctions in the Frog's Language: Fill-in Drill

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.57): choose and, or, but, because to fill blanks in frog-themed sentences.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes one example sentence on the board using a word from the poem — 'I live on land ___ water too' — and invites students to suggest what word fits. The teacher introduces 'and', 'or', 'but', and 'because' as joining words with a one-sentence explanation of each.

Let us Learn — A. (p.57): the teacher reads sentence 1 aloud ('My colours match the plants ___ trees') and the two bracket choices. Students think, then respond. The teacher confirms 'and' and shows why 'or' would change the meaning.

Let us Learn — A. (p.57): sentences 2, 3, and 4 are worked through one at a time — teacher reads, students write their chosen word on a slate or paper, and the class compares. The teacher explains each answer by pointing to the relationship the joining word creates.

Students form pairs and each pair makes one new sentence using any of the four joining words, with a frog or animal as the subject. Three or four pairs share their sentences aloud; the class identifies the joining word used.

periods.teacher_notes: The conjunction 'because' is the most challenging here — students often confuse it with 'so'. Use sentence 4 ('Frogs swim easily because they have webbed feet') to illustrate the cause-effect direction: 'because' introduces the reason. Keeping all four sentences visible on the board during the pair-making activity helps students see the pattern.
materials: Slates or rough paper for drafting

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.57–58): choose correctly arranged sentences from jumbled animal words.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes a short jumbled word string on the board (e.g. 'pond/sits/in/frog/the') and invites a volunteer to arrange it into a proper sentence. The class confirms; the teacher briefly names what a well-ordered sentence needs (subject, verb, rest).

Let us Learn — B. (pp.57–58): the teacher reads item 1 (tiger/hunt scramble) aloud and all three options. Students vote by raising a finger for A, B, or C. After the vote, the teacher explains why 'The tiger hunts silently at night' is the correct order.

Let us Learn — B. (pp.57–58): items 2, 3, and 4 (elephants, spider, crocodile) are worked through in the same vote-and-explain pattern. Students write their answers on slates or paper before the class vote to keep thinking individual.

Let us Learn — B. (pp.57–58): item 5 (turtle sentence) is completed; then students pair up and create their own one-sentence scramble about any animal. Partners swap and rearrange each other's scrambles and share aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The common error in sentence-ordering is placing adverbs ('silently') before the subject — students may produce 'Silently the tiger hunts at night' as a plausible distractor. Accept it as understandable but guide students to the most natural English order used in the options. The pair-scramble extension at the end gives students ownership over the grammatical principle.

periods.activity_title: Writing Back to Hopper: A Letter in Reply

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (pp.59–60): read Hopper's letter; plan, draft, and share a reply letter in the notebook.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads Hopper's letter aloud from the textbook (pp.59–60) with warmth and expression. Students listen and follow. The teacher draws attention to the letter's structure: greeting, body with hobby and favourite food, question, sign-off.

The teacher models a short reply on the board — greeting ('Dear Hopper'), one sentence about a personal hobby, one sentence about a favourite food, a question back to Hopper, and a sign-off. Students observe and note the structure without copying.

Let us Write (pp.59–60): students draft their own reply to Hopper in their notebooks. The teacher circulates, prompting with 'What is one thing YOU like to do?' and 'What would you ask a frog?' to support students who are stuck.

Three or four volunteers read their reply letters aloud to the class. After each reading, one classmate says one thing they liked about the letter. The teacher acknowledges the range of personal details students included.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes write a reply that merely repeats Hopper's facts back to him — nudge them toward genuine personal content by asking what THEY like and what they would want to tell a frog. Remind students that Hopper asked 'What do you like to do?' — their letter should answer that question. The letter should be brief, around three to five sentences, written and shared within this sitting.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — A. (p.62): find five hidden frogs in the nature-scene picture.
Let us Do — C. (p.64): move three crayons to change the direction of the fish shape.

time_bands.activity: The teacher connects today's activities to the poem's camouflage image — 'I hide so well in grass and leaves!' — and tells students they will now see that camouflage in action. Students open textbooks to p.62.

Let us Do — A. (p.62): students examine the nature-scene picture individually and try to find all five hidden frogs. After individual search, pairs compare findings. The teacher confirms each frog's location and discusses how the frog's colours help it hide.

The teacher introduces the crayon-fish puzzle on p.64 and explains the rule: move exactly three crayons (or sticks) to make the fish swim the other way. Students work in pairs using pencils or sticks on their desks to try different arrangements.

Let us Do — C. (p.64): pairs share their solutions. The teacher demonstrates the correct three-move solution if no pair has found it, thinking aloud through each step. Students discuss what kind of thinking the puzzle uses.

periods.teacher_notes: The hidden-frog activity directly illustrates the poem's camouflage theme and rewards careful, patient looking rather than speed — encourage students who find fewer frogs quickly to describe what they are scanning for. The crayon puzzle is a spatial-reasoning challenge; if students are stuck, suggest they start by deciding which direction the fish must face at the end, then work backwards.
materials: Pencils or small sticks for the crayon puzzle

periods.activity_title: Drawing a Duck and Exploring Ocean Creatures

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — B. (p.63): follow five-step diagram to draw a duck in the given space.
Let us Explore (p.64): choose two sea creatures and share two or three facts about each.

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students what they notice is similar between a duck and a frog — both live near water, both have webbed feet. This brief conversation links the drawing task to the poem's world.

Let us Do — B. (p.63): the teacher walks through the five-step drawing diagram on p.63 one step at a time, drawing on the board while students follow in their textbooks. Students complete each step in the given space, pausing after each board demonstration.

Let us Explore (p.64): the teacher displays or reads aloud the list of sea creatures (Puffer fish, Jellyfish, Seahorse, Starfish, Octopus, Catfish) and each student silently picks two. They spend a few minutes thinking of any facts they know about their chosen creatures from books, TV, or experience.

Students share two or three facts about their chosen creatures in a quick round — each student names their two creatures and one fact per creature. The teacher notes any especially surprising facts on the board and celebrates curiosity.

periods.teacher_notes: The step-by-step drawing is a sequential-instruction task — students who rush ahead and skip a step often end up with a lopsided duck; encourage them to wait for each board step. For the Let us Explore sharing, accept any reasonable fact from experience or general knowledge; the goal is building curiosity about water creatures, not factual precision. Students who cannot recall facts may describe what the creature looks like.
materials: Pencils and coloured pencils for drawing

periods.activity_title: The Frog Comes Together: Whole-Chapter Synthesis

time_bands.activity: Students open their textbooks to pp.55–56. The class reads the full poem aloud together, chorally, in a confident final reading. The teacher invites students to notice the rhyming couplet pattern and the hopping rhythm before they begin.

Whole-class retell in a circle: each student contributes one thing the frog does, feels, or says in the poem, drawing on the poem's images — darting tongue, webbed feet, camouflage, croaking songs. No repeats are allowed; the round continues until the circle runs out of new ideas.

Students write three sentences in their notebooks describing the frog's life, using at least one conjunction (and, but, because, or) in each sentence. The teacher circulates and invites students to read a sentence aloud if their conjunction is used well.

The teacher poses two riddle-style questions aloud: 'I croak my songs and hide in leaves — what am I?' and 'I started life as a tiny fish-like thing — what am I now?' Students answer and then make up one riddle of their own about any creature from the chapter's world, sharing with a partner.

The teacher closes by asking students to name one thing they remember most vividly from the chapter — a line, an image, a word, or a fact — and shares one themselves. This brief round-the-room closing celebrates the chapter's ideas without requiring any particular prior activity to have happened.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together the poem's language (reading), the frog's story (oracy), conjunctions (word work), short independent writing, and the riddle spirit of the beyond-text activities. Because any unit of this chapter may have been a student's only sitting, the activities here are grounded entirely in the poem text itself and need no earlier draft, chart, or artwork to be present. Accept a wide range of responses in the retell and riddle rounds — richness here shows how much of the frog's world students have made their own.

items.item_stem: Read the opening lines of the poem beginning "I sit in ponds and in the rain." Which of the following best describes the places where the frog lives and spends time?

options.label: A
options.text: Only in ponds and rivers deep in the forest.

options.label: B
options.text: In ponds, muddy drains, and damp places with drops of dew.

options.label: C
options.text: In tall trees and dry, sunny meadows.

options.label: D
options.text: Only in muddy drains near human homes.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students choosing this may recall 'pond' from the poem but have added 'rivers' from outside knowledge, missing the drain and dew details.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a confusion between the frog's world and a land animal's habitat; the student has not attended to the poem's water and damp imagery.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows the student noticed 'muddy drain' but overgeneralised it, missing the broader range of habitats the poem describes.

items.item_stem: The poem describes two ways the frog protects itself and moves through its world — its camouflage and its webbed feet. In two or three sentences, explain what the frog's colours do for it and how its webbed feet help it, using details from the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The frog's colours match the plants and trees around it, so it can hide well in grass and leaves. Its webbed feet help it swim with ease in the water.

items.source_context: Frog's amphibious life, hopping ability, frog-versus-fish comparison, webbed-feet and flipper analogy.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the following two statements about the frog and the fish. Decide whether each statement is true or false.
1. A fish can live on land as well as in water, just like the frog in the poem.
2. The frog in the poem uses its webbed feet to swim, which is similar to how scuba divers use flippers.

options.text: A fish can live on land as well as in water, just like the frog in the poem.
The frog in the poem uses its webbed feet to swim, which is similar to how scuba divers use flippers.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is false: the poem describes the frog as living on both land and water, but a fish lives only in water. Statement 2 is true: the poem says the frog swims with ease using its webbed feet, and scuba divers use flippers in the same way to propel themselves through water.

items.source_lo: Student expresses imaginative comparisons and personal responses through guided oral discussion using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Frog's amphibious life, hopping ability, frog-versus-fish comparison, webbed-feet and flipper analogy.
items.item_stem: Imagine you could live like the frog in the poem — spending time both in water and on land, hopping to great heights, and singing your own songs. Tell your partner or your teacher: what is one thing you would enjoy most about a frog's life, and one thing that would be difficult? Use ideas from the poem to explain your answer.

expected_elements: Names one enjoyable aspect from the poem.
Names one genuine difficulty from the poem.
Uses at least one specific poem detail.

items.item_stem: Hopper the frog wrote a letter saying his favourite hobby is sitting in water puddles and croaking, and that he loves eating mosquitoes. He ended his letter with: "What do you like to do?" Read this sentence from Hopper's letter and write one sentence that answers his question, using a proper letter greeting to start.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: A complete response begins with a greeting (e.g. 'Dear Hopper,') and contains one sentence answering Hopper's question with a personal activity or hobby.

items.item_stem: Write a short reply letter to Hopper the frog. In your letter, include: a greeting to Hopper, one thing you enjoy doing, one question you want to ask Hopper about his life in the pond, and a friendly sign-off. Your letter should be three to five sentences long.

expected_elements: Includes a proper greeting and sign-off.
Shares one personal hobby or favourite thing.
